`--request-file` is optional. Without it the requirement is the one of the last accepted (`auto_approve`) review of this
repository and branch: every accepted review stores its requirement text byte for byte as `request.txt` beside its record under
`~/.local/share/clouseau/reviews/<cache id>/`, with a `requirement.json` that binds it, and one pointer per repository and
branch (`requirements/`) names the newest. The command refuses, and asks for `--request-file`, when nothing is recorded for the
branch, when the record is unusable (pointer and record name different repositories, branches, heads or cache ids; the text no
longer hashes to the recorded digest; a part is a link, empty or over 20,000 characters), when the recorded head is not an
ancestor of the pull request head, or is already in the base (the branch name was reused after another pull request merged), or when that review also used
`--additional-checks` (they are part of its input and are not stored; pass both again). It never guesses among candidates.
Optional: `--directory`, `--identity`, `--additional-checks`, `--engine latest`. In order, and never otherwise:

1. refuse (see below), then `git fetch origin <base>`; if the pull request already contains the base tip, the receipt in the
   pull request body decides: one that still verifies for this head ends the command with `up_to_date`, any other is
   [renewed](#renewing-a-receipt-that-no-longer-verifies) (steps 3 to 5 below, no merge and no push of the branch). Under the
   protected `binding: "diff"`, when the pull request does not contain the base tip and its receipt still covers its diff, the
   base is merged and the normalized diff recomputed; if it is unchanged the merge is pushed with no review and the command
   ends with `updated` (see [Binding a receipt to its diff](#binding-a-receipt-to-its-diff-opt-in)); otherwise the steps
   continue on that merge;
2. check with `git merge-tree` that the merge is clean, then **merge** the base (`git merge --no-ff`, message
   `Merge origin/<base> into <branch>`). There is no rebase and no force-push anywhere in the command;
3. run the ordinary local review of the head (`clouseau review`, including its verification) with the answers reused as
   described below, and sign the receipt. The claimed title of the change is the pull request's own title (GitHub's), not the
   subject of the merge commit, which is only `Merge origin/<base> into <branch>`; a pull request with no title is refused;
4. `clouseau publish` the receipt (this pushes only the artifact tag `clouseau-review/<nonce>`);
5. replace the `clouseau-local-review:v1` marker in the pull request body (appended when there is none);
6. `git push origin HEAD:<pull request branch>`, once, as the last step.

It refuses, with a message that names the cause and before pushing anything, when: the worktree has uncommitted or untracked
changes; HEAD is not the head GitHub reports for the pull request (when the local branch only has commits on top of that head, the message
says how many are unpushed and that you must `git push` first, then refresh again); the pull request is closed, comes from a fork, is not the
checked-out branch, or is not against the configured `base_branch`; the harness is unknown or its program is not installed;
the base conflicts with the branch (the checkout is left untouched and the conflicting paths are listed); a hook refuses the
merge (it is aborted). It never pushes when the review does not pass (`repair_required`, `review_incomplete`, ...), when a
passing review produced no signed receipt (no enrolled identity), when the checkout changed during the review, when the
pull request closed or got another head during the review, or when the push is rejected (the body is then restored). After
a review that does not pass, the merge commit stays in the local branch: repair, commit and refresh again, or run `git reset
--hard <old head>` to discard it. An agent-driven refresh that returns `awaiting_agent` is repeated with the identical
command; it recognises its own merge commit (the pull request head and a commit of the base as parents), does not merge or
fetch again, and continues on the base it began with. While Clouseau main advances, the continuation runs on the engine revision
that started the exchange ([pinning](#agent-driven-review-inside-an-ai-harness)): through the `clouseau` launcher the pinned engine
receives your own `refresh` command, resumes it and finishes it (review, publication, marker, push), and its result is what you
see. If the pinned engine fails, its error message is shown.

### Binding a receipt to its diff (opt-in)

By default a receipt is bound to the exact head and base commits it reviewed, so every merge to the base voids the receipt of
every other open pull request. With the protected `local_review.binding: "diff"` in `.github/clouseau.json` on the base branch,
a receipt is bound to the **change** instead: it covers a pull request when the SHA-256 of the pull request's normalized diff
equals the SHA-256 of the normalized diff in the signed record (`src/receipt-patch.cjs`). The receipt format does not change:
the signed record already carries every patch.

The normalized diff is, per changed file in path order, its path, its status and (for a rename) its previous path, and its
hunks with every hunk header reduced to `@@`, so line numbers and git's trailing section text do not count. Every other byte
of a hunk counts, context lines and whitespace included. GitHub joins two git hunks that are one unchanged line apart; that
run of exactly seven context lines between two changes is split back into its two hunks on both sides. A summarized lockfile
contributes its path and status, and its derived summary is recomputed from the live lockfile bytes and must equal the signed
one apart from the revision it names.

| | Binding absent | `binding: "diff"` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a different head commit (GitHub's branch update, a merge of the base) | `receipt_revision_head` | covered while the diff is unchanged |
| a different base commit | `receipt_revision_base` | covered while the diff is unchanged |
| signed full-file sources compared with the live repository | compared | not compared: the signed record is what was reviewed; each source must still name a signed revision |
| the repository's contracts (`readme`, `repository_policy`, for example `.github/clouseau.md` and `README.md`) | compared at the signed base, which must be the live base | compared at the **live** base: a base move that changed either voids the receipt (`receipt_source`, naming the file) |
| lines added above a hunk on the base | `receipt_source` | covered |
| any change to an added, removed or context line, or to whitespace | `receipt_source` | `receipt_source`, naming the file |
| a file added, removed or re-statused, another rename | refused | refused, unchanged |
| a compatibility declaration (`compat/declarations/<sha256>.json`) declared again after a merge | refused (its bytes changed) | covered while every declaration keeps its verdict over the same files (path, mode, deleted or not); only the content digests it pins may differ |
| a file without a GitHub patch | refused, unless the live sources prove it shows no text | refused, even an empty file or an identical rename: the live sources are not read |
| signature, enrolled key, author, expiry, repository, protected configuration and policy digests, engine and review semantics, passing decision | bound | bound, unchanged |

A compatibility declaration ([receipt compatibility](receipt-compatibility.md)) pins the full content of the semantic files
it covers. When the base gains a merged pull request that changed one of those files, merging the base makes the
declaration stale, and declaring again replaces it with a new file under a new name. Under the binding that replacement does
not void the receipt: a file added under exactly `compat/declarations/<64 hex>.json` whose whole content is a well-formed
declaration is compared by what it declares, its verdict (`compatible` or `incompatible`) and the files it covers with their
mode and whether each is deleted, and it is left out of the normalized diff. A changed verdict, a file added to or removed
from a declaration, or a declaration gained or lost voids the receipt (`receipt_source`). Any other file under that directory
(another name, another status, a body that is not one whole declaration) is an ordinary changed file. The required `verify`
job still checks every declaration against the merged tree, so a declaration whose digests do not match the code fails
there. The pull request's changed-file count still includes the declarations.

**What still voids a diff-bound receipt after a base move.** A change on the base branch to the repository's contracts
(`readme` and `repository_policy`, compared at the live base) or to the declared recipe (`.clouseau-local.json`, which the
test waiver compares at the live base) voids every open diff-bound receipt, by design: the change was judged against them. A
summarized lockfile's summary is recomputed from the live base and head lockfile bytes, so a base move that changed a
lockfile the pull request also changes voids it when the recomputed summary differs.

The test waiver follows the same binding: `operation: attested` answers `'true'` for a receipt whose diff matches and whose
signed `.clouseau-local.json` equals the live base's, so the tests are **not** rerun after a base move or an update-branch
merge. This is deliberate and has a cost: a break caused only by the base move (a semantic conflict between the reviewed change
and the new base) is found after merge, by the next run on the base. **Accepted limit:** no CI step reruns the attested tests
of a diff-bound receipt for any base move, including one that changed a file the pull request imports or calls but does not
edit; only a change to the declared recipe (`.clouseau-local.json`) or to the pull request's own diff makes CI run them. The run-consistency checks that compare the live pull
request between the assessment and the gate are unchanged; they protect one CI run from a push that lands mid-run.

`clouseau refresh` uses the same decision: under the binding it judges the receipt (including the diff, from the files GitHub
lists) before merging anything. When it stands, refresh merges the base locally and recomputes the normalized diff: if it
equals the diff before the merge (the base moved elsewhere, or on lines of a changed file outside every hunk), refresh pushes
the merge (a plain push, never forced) with no review and no new receipt, and answers `updated`. That keeps the branch strictly
ahead of the base, which the controller-managed merge requires. Only when the merge changed the diff (the base moved a line
inside a hunk's context) does refresh review the merged head, as it does without the binding. On an up-to-date branch it answers `up_to_date` whenever CI would accept the receipt. Who
updates the branch is therefore the author: by `clouseau refresh`, by GitHub's "Update branch" (`gh pr update-branch`), or by a
plain merge and push; the workflow token cannot, because its push starts no verification. A merge commit that leaves the
diff unchanged keeps the receipt valid end to end, at the assessment and at the gate (`verifyRecord`, and `verifySources` at
the gate's write boundary), which `src/acceptance-controller-binding.test.cjs` proves through an assessment and gate approval
of the merged head with zero AI calls. A receipt that no longer covers the diff is refreshed or renewed as usual.

`updated` never pushes a head that fails a cheap deterministic invariant of the repository; it does not run the verification
recipe. In a repository with compatibility declarations (a `compat/manifest.json` and a `compat/declarations/` directory,
as in Clouseau's own; see [receipt compatibility](receipt-compatibility.md#declare-then-fold)), refresh checks the merged tree
with the same `inspect` as `scripts/review-compatibility verify` before the push. When the merge only changed a file the pull
request declared, so its declaration pins stale content, and the stale declarations cover exactly the pull request's own
changed semantic files with one decision, refresh replaces them with one declaration of that decision over the same files,
commits it as `chore(compat): re-pin the compatibility declaration after merging origin/<base>` and pushes both commits; the
result then carries `declaration: "re-pinned"`. Any other finding (a different path set, an undeclared change, mixed
decisions, or a base change to a declared file that is not folded yet) pushes nothing and names the cause; the merge commit
stays in the local branch. A repository without that tooling is refreshed exactly as before.

The owner's `/approve-intent` (and an approving review) names one exact head, under the binding too, unless the protected
`local_review.confirmation: "diff"` is set as well (it is valid only together with `binding: "diff"`). With it, a
confirmation of an earlier head (comment or approving review) also counts for the current head when that earlier commit was
this pull request's: an ancestor of the head, or, after a rebase, a commit that one of the pull request's force pushes
replaced or produced or an ancestor of one. The engine reads those force pushes itself from the pull request's timeline
(`HeadRefForcePushedEvent`), never from comment text; more than 100 force pushes, or a commit GitHub no longer has, does
not carry. In addition, its normalized diff (taken from its merge base with the live base) equals the pull request's
current diff, and its merge base carries the same `.github/clouseau.json` and purpose contract (`repository_policy`) as the
live base. A merge of the base or a rebase onto it that leaves the change unchanged therefore keeps the confirmation; any push
that changes the diff (a new commit, or a conflict resolution that alters the branch's own lines), and any base change to
the protected configuration or the contract, voids it. A base change that edits the lines around the branch's own change
changes the diff's context lines, so it voids the confirmation too; a change elsewhere in the same file only moves the
hunk offsets, which the normalized diff ignores. A patchless or truncated file list, an
unknown commit or another lineage never matches, and any other API failure surfaces. The comment itself stays exactly
`/approve-intent <sha>`. The recorded authorization names the head it was applied to and, when that differs, the
`confirmed_sha` it was given for. Without the setting, a confirmation names the exact head, as before. Where the binding applies: `verifySignedRecord` (the head and base comparison),
`verifySources` (revisions, sources, contract and verification refs, the lockfile summary, and the diff through `verifyPatches`),
and through them `screenReceipt`, `screenSources`, `receiptAttests`, `rehydrate` and `verifyRecord` (the record's revisions), and
`receipt-standing.cjs` and `pr-refresh.cjs`. An installation receipt is never diff-bound.

### Base moved: hold or update (opt-in)

When the base moves after a pull request was assessed and only the base differs (the live head is still the assessed head), the
gate stops. The protected `local_review.base_moved` in `.github/clouseau.json` on the base branch says what it does then. It is
valid only together with `binding: "diff"` (any other combination, or a value other than these two, fails configuration
validation, like `confirmation`):

| `base_moved` | The gate, after a base-only move |
| --- | --- |
| absent or `"hold"` (the default) | posts the `base_moved` needs-branch-update notice and fails, exactly as before; the owner updates the branch |
| `"update"` | for an approved revision (a decision of `auto_approve` or `owner_decision` and, where the gate requires a maintainer's confirmation: the owner decision itself, a protected path or a bot-authored pull request, that confirmation of this head), merges the base into the branch server-side (`updateBranch` with `expected_head_sha`), posts no notice, and ends the job with cause `base_update_requested` (`Branch updated server-side ...`): this revision is neither approved nor merged, and the new head's own run continues. Anything else (another decision, or a confirmation still outstanding) posts the notice and fails, as under `"hold"`: Clouseau never merges the base into a branch that is not yet approved |

The update needs the gate step's `update-token` input: a token whose push **starts workflows**, with contents: write on the
repository (a fine-grained PAT or an App token, like `repair-token`; the reference template passes the same
`CLOUSEAU_REPAIR_TOKEN` secret to both). When the base brings changes to `.github/workflows/`, GitHub also requires workflows
permission (workflows: write for a fine-grained token or App, the `workflow` scope for a classic token). Without it GitHub
refuses the update and the gate fails with that refusal, updating nothing. The workflow `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot be used: a push made with it starts no workflow, so
the new head would have no verification. Without `update-token` the gate holds as under `"hold"`, and the notice says to set
the `update-token` input of the gate step. A head in a fork is never updated (the notice says so). When GitHub refuses with
HTTP 422 (a merge conflict with the base, or a head that moved) the gate falls back to the notice, which says so and asks the
owner to update by hand; any other refusal fails the job with GitHub's error. Under `"update"`, `reconcile-base` also updates
**every** stale same-repository pull request in one run instead of one at a time, because under the diff binding a base-only
update needs no fresh review; under `"hold"` it is unchanged. A repository that does not set `base_moved` is unaffected even
when the token is supplied.

**What runs on the updated head.** The new head's own `pull_request` run. Its `attested` job answers `'true'` while the
diff-bound receipt still attests (the diff is unchanged and the base's `.clouseau-local.json` is the signed one), so `verify`
skips every receipt-covered step; only steps outside the receipt's recipe still run (none in the reference template; this
repository's own engine self-tests, for example). Then the assessment reuses the receipt with zero CI AI calls: no reviewer is
asked, and under `confirmation: "diff"` the owner's confirmation carries. The receipt-covered commands are **not** re-run on
the base merged with the branch. This is the same outcome as `clouseau refresh` answering `updated` today, with the same
accepted limit (see the test waiver above): a break caused only by the base move is found after merge. When the merge changed
the diff, the receipt no longer covers it and the new head is verified and reviewed as any new head.

**Loop bound.** The update is requested only when the live head equals the assessed head and only the base moved, and
`expected_head_sha` makes GitHub refuse if the head moved meanwhile. A rerun of the old head's gate sees the new head, so it
is not a base-only move and requests nothing: the same (head, base) is updated at most once. The new head's assessment carries
the new base, so it requests another update only if the base moves again. Updating a branch never moves the base, so two pull
requests cannot update each other. `src/acceptance-controller-base-moved.test.cjs` and `src/base-reconcile-base-moved.test.cjs`
prove these at the gate (both base-move checks, including the private-merge boundary) and at reconciliation.

### Renewing a receipt that no longer verifies

When the base has not moved (or, under the diff binding, at any time), `refresh` does not answer `up_to_date` merely because nothing needs merging. It judges the
`clouseau-local-review:` marker in the pull request body for the unchanged head exactly as CI does: the same screening code
(`screenReceipt`, with the same signature, author, expiry, repository, head, base, protected configuration and policy, engine
and review-semantics checks) on the pull request as GitHub reports it now, the protected `.github/clouseau.json` of the fetched
base, and the engine that is running. The receipt is read through `gh api` from the immutable commit the marker names; nothing
in the marker or the receipt is trusted before it verifies. A repository whose protected configuration has no `local_review`
section has no receipts to judge and keeps the plain `up_to_date`.

- **The receipt verifies**: `up_to_date`, `pushed: false`; nothing is reviewed, published or edited.
- **It does not** (expired, issued against another base or head (without the diff binding) or for another diff, for another repository or author, signed by a key that is not
  enrolled, an engine that is not accepted, a malformed, unreadable or forged marker, more than one marker, or no marker): the
  command prints the cause on stderr (`Renewing the local review receipt of pull request N (cause: receipt_expired): it is expired
  or not yet valid (it expires <instant>)`; the classes are those of [receipt notices](notices.md)) and performs steps 3 to 5 for
  the current head: the ordinary local review with the stored-requirement default and the evidence-keyed reuse described below
  (an unchanged head is mostly answered from the remembered reviews), the receipt, its publication and the marker in the pull
  request body. It does **not** merge and does **not** push the branch, whose head is unchanged; the only push is the artifact
  tag of step 4. The result has `status: "renewed"`, `pushed: false`, `cause` and `reason`, the new `marker` and `artifact_commit`.
  An agent-driven renewal that returns `awaiting_agent` is repeated with the identical command like any other.

The same refusals apply as for a merge (dirty worktree, HEAD not the pull request head, missing harness, fork, wrong branch or
base, no requirement), a review that does not pass or is not signed publishes and edits nothing, and a failure to read the
receipt that is not the receipt's own (GitHub unreachable) stops the command instead of guessing. A receipt can never be
renewed without a new review: an expired receipt cached by `clouseau review` for the same input is retired (its stored
requirement stays) and the input is reviewed again. Publishing a receipt whose artifact tag is already on the remote with the
same files reuses that artifact (for example when only the marker was lost); a tag with other content is refused, and a tag is
never overwritten.

### What is reused

A review asks the harness one question at a time (each unit investigation, each integration pass, each grading round). A review
that ends `auto_approve` remembers every answer in `~/.local/share/clouseau/unit-reuse/`, under the digest of the question's
complete input. `refresh` (and `clouseau review` under the opt-in outcome keying below) lets a question take a remembered answer instead of asking again, when its input
is **byte-identical** to the remembered one except for the values that name the revision rather than describe it. The input
covers the policy and stage text, the schema, role and phase, every changed patch, every base and head source, every
source that was requested or linked, the change manifest and seams, the requirement, the prior findings, the verification
record, the configuration and policy digests, the commit ids of each file's recent history and the review semantics of the
engine (`review-semantics.cjs`). Any change to any of them is a different key and the question is asked. The excluded values,
replaced by placeholders on both sides of the comparison, are: the base and head commit ids, the snapshot and unit-view
digests, the claimed title of the change (a claim, never proof; a refresh uses the pull request's title) and, for a verification command that passed, its
output tails and output digests (its argv, exit code, coverage counters and configuration digest stay in the key; a failed
command is compared byte for byte). A reused answer is put through the same check as a fresh one against the new snapshot, and
is asked again when that check fails; the receipt is signed over the new head, base and evidence, and CI verifies it exactly
as before. In a chunked review the same holds per call (every unit, integration pass and grading round), but every unit also
sees the change manifest of the whole change (each changed path with its line counts and size), so a base movement that
changes any changed file asks every unit again, while one that touches none of them reuses all of them. The result reports
`reused_calls` and `harness_invocations` (calls actually made).

Limits to expect: a changed requirement text, policy, contract, verification command or engine semantics reuses nothing; a
verification that fails reuses nothing about its output; the store is not pruned and may be deleted at any time. See
[binding a receipt to its diff](#binding-a-receipt-to-its-diff-opt-in) for letting CI keep a receipt when the base moved.

### Reusing answers in `clouseau review` (opt-in)

By default only `refresh` reads the store, and the coverage counters of the verification record are part of every key. A
base that added code anywhere changes those counters, so a later review after merging it asks every question again even
when nothing the reviewers judge has changed.

Two equivalent switches opt a review in to **outcome keying**:
- `clouseau review --reuse outcome`, for one run;
- `"review_reuse": "outcome"` in `.clouseau-local.json`, read from the base like the rest of that file, for every review
  and refresh. It is a protected control.
`--reuse` and the field accept only `"outcome"`; anything else is refused. With either switch:

- `clouseau review` reads the store as `refresh` does.
- Exact coverage that is complete (every line and branch counter covered) is keyed as `complete`, not by its counts.
  Coverage that is not complete keeps its counters in the key, as does every byte of a failed command.
- Everything else in the key is unchanged. A base move that touches a changed file (its base text or its recent history),
  a new commit on the branch, a changed requirement, policy, contract, configuration or engine semantics, still asks
  again. Outcome keys name their keying, so an answer stored under one keying is never read under the other.
- Verification always runs again on the reviewed tree; only the reviewers' answers are reused, and each still passes the
  same check against the new snapshot.
- The signed receipt carries the claim `"review_reuse": {"mode": "outcome", "reused": N, "fresh": M}`: how many reviewer
  calls were taken from the store and how many were asked. A receipt without the claim was made without outcome keying.
  CI accepts only that exact shape.

What it gives up: the reviewers no longer see a change in the coverage counts as evidence while coverage stays complete.
The verdict they judge (all commands passed, coverage exact) is the same either way.

## Maintainer attestation of another author's pull request (opt-in)

By default the enrolled signing key's `github_actor` must equal the pull request
author exactly, so a pull request by Dependabot or an outside contributor can never
carry a receipt. A repository can opt in, in the protected base configuration only:

```json
"local_review": {"...": "...", "attest": {"authors": ["dependabot[bot]", "a-named-contributor"]}}
```

`authors` is either a nonempty list of distinct, exact logins (an app account keeps
its `[bot]` suffix; matching is exact and case-sensitive) or the explicit string
`"any"`. An empty list, a missing `authors`, any other value or any other field makes
the configuration invalid. Without `attest` nothing changes: behavior is byte-identical
and the author must equal the signer's login. The setting lives in the protected
configuration, so a pull request cannot enable it for itself, and it is part of the
configuration digest every receipt binds.

The maintainer checks out exactly the pull request head (`git fetch origin
pull/N/head && git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD`, the same ref for forks) and runs
the ordinary review with the extra option `--pr N`:

```bash
clouseau review --directory . --base origin/main --request-file req.txt --agent claude --pr N
clouseau publish --directory . --receipt PATH_FROM_THE_REVIEW_OUTPUT
```

The CLI asks GitHub (`gh api`) for the pull request's author, open state, base branch
and head. It refuses unless attestation is enabled, the pull request is open against
the base branch, HEAD is exactly the pull request head and the author is allowed. A
pull request the signer authored needs no attestation and is signed as before. The
signer runs the repository's verification commands on code the author wrote;
review the change before running it on a workstation you care about.

The signed payload then carries `attestation: {author, number, signer}`. CI accepts
it only when all of these hold: the key is enrolled and active, the protected
configuration allows that pull request's author, the signed author equals the pull
request author, the signed signer equals the key's enrolled login, and the signed
number equals the pull request number. A receipt signed for one author or pull
request therefore cannot be replayed for another, and a verifier without `attest`
(including installation trust) rejects every attested receipt. Reasons use the fixed
class `attestation`. The pull request comment and job summary say
`Maintainer-attested`, name the signer and author, and the assessment's
`review_source` is `maintainer_attested`.

An attested receipt is exactly as strong as any other: it never authorizes a change
to protected review controls (`/approve-intent` is still required and unchanged),
tests and exact coverage still must pass, and a push to the pull request head makes
it stale. A bot that rewrites the pull request body or rebases (Dependabot does)
removes the marker or the matching head, so publish for the final head and place the
marker last.

## CI consumes evidence without repeating AI

An opted-in protected workflow loads configuration and Clouseau from trusted
source. It loads a referenced receipt as data, validates its
signature/issuer/author/time/revisions/policy, compares the complete signed source
inventory to GitHub's immutable PR sources (dependency lockfile summaries are
recomputed from the repository's lockfile bytes and must match exactly), and
recalculates the AI scores.
A valid local assessment can be authenticated and reused with zero CI AI calls
even while independent CI is pending or failed. That result remains
`pending_technical` or `blocked_technical`, with no approval-usable record digest
or approval/merge write. Unstamped PRs retain the CI provider route after
technical verification.

### Reviewed diff verification

CI also verifies the diff text the reviewers saw. It reuses the changed-file list
already fetched for the assessment (the pull request files endpoint, paginated;
no extra request per file) and compares each file's repository-supplied `patch`
with the signed `snapshot.files[].patch`. The local collector stores `git diff`
output, so the comparison reduces it to GitHub's form: the git extended header
(`diff --git`, mode, similarity, rename, `index`, `---`, `+++` lines) is removed
and the final newline dropped; every remaining byte of the hunks must equal what
GitHub reports. A header line that is not one of those git lines, or a rename
that is not the pull request's rename, is a mismatch. Whitespace-only differences
are mismatches. The file list and each file's status must match exactly: no extra
file, none missing.

Any disagreement means the receipt does not verify: it is ignored (class `source`)
and CI reviews the change itself, as described under
[a receipt that does not verify is ignored](#a-receipt-that-does-not-verify-is-ignored).
No file name or diff content is forwarded. GitHub supplies no `patch` for very large or binary changes. The
hosted collector already refuses those (`changed_files_incomplete`), and CI refuses
the same changes with that cause rather than verifying a receipt with a weaker rule.

GitHub also supplies no `patch` for a change that shows no text: an empty file added or removed (a Python
`__init__.py`), or a rename of identical content. Both collectors accept that, and only that, when the immutable
sources prove it (the head source of an added file is empty, the base source of a removed file is empty, or the
two sides of a rename are equal). A signed `git diff` of such a file is a header without a hunk and equals the absent
hosted patch. An empty source has no line to cite, so the review accounts for it without a citation, a finding is
anchored in the next changed file that has a line, and any other missing patch still fails closed. A receipt bound
by `binding: "diff"` never covers a file without a patch, because the live sources that would prove it empty are not read.

Only after actual CI tests and exact coverage pass may the controller emit an
approval assessment. It revalidates the receipt at the write gate and uses the
existing native approval, merge-authority and protection checks. Missing, stale,
revoked, altered, non-passing or unauthorized receipts cannot approve; one that
does not verify is ignored and CI performs every check itself.

Tests, exact 100% coverage and the applicable shared protection/owner-merge
rules remain mandatory before approval or merge. Review-control changes retain
their existing exact-revision owner installation requirements.
Post-deployment wiki generation and factual review remain separate operations.

Local caches include the exact installed central SHA, even when a newer commit
has identical engine bytes. Refreshing and reviewing again creates evidence for
that new SHA and preserves the old receipt. An exact matching cached receipt
still avoids another local review. Negative evidence and causal findings remain
retained; a different SHA with identical engine bytes cannot resample an unchanged
negative judgment.

When a resolver workflow changes, the runner supplies at most 32 observed shared
source/test dependencies, its actual bootstrap and the legacy action
boundary as additional untrusted context. Wiki source is included only when the
changed workflow invokes it.
Historical source requests use `.clouseau-ci/PATH@FULL_COMMIT_SHA`; they read
immutable public bytes without switching the frozen review engine or granting
contract authority. CI checks the same bytes before receipt reuse. The ordinary
serialized evidence size remains capped at 900,000 characters. Each local
investigation can read eight batches of
up to eight paths, then submit its report using the final batch. A ninth source
batch still stops the review; missing evidence cannot produce a passing report.
Failed investigations retain `snapshot.json`
and `observations.jsonl`; their error gives the evidence directory. These files
contain review evidence, never the signing identity.

Automatic central-source installations retain signer enrollment in protected base
configuration and authorize protected Clouseau main instead of a recurring
reviewer digest. A receipt produced by an older engine revision than the protected
main CI resolved is one more receipt that does not verify (class `engine`, below).
Refresh and review again to reuse the local review. The selected commit and digest are in
the run summary and engine artifact.

### Signing a review that requires a human (opt-in)

By default only a passing local review is signed. The protected `local_review.human_review` in `.github/clouseau.json` on
the base branch accepts exactly one value, `"signed"`; any other value (an empty string, `true`, `null`, another word) makes
the configuration invalid (`human_review must be "signed" when set`). Absent, nothing changes: only a passing review is
ever signed.

With `"signed"`, `clouseau review` also signs a review whose only blocker is graded findings:

| Local result | Signed outcome |
| --- | --- |
| tests or the coverage gate fail | nothing (no review is run) |
| test integrity violated (`blocked_integrity`) | nothing |
| another gate violated or unresolved (scope, security, compatibility, completeness), with or without findings | nothing |
| an earlier blocking finding neither retained nor resolved | nothing (the review is incomplete) |
| findings at or above the threshold, every gate of both reviews satisfied or inapplicable (`repair_required`) | the review, signed with its findings |
| clean | the passing review, as today |

`issueReceipt` enforces the same rule as `clouseau review`, so no other caller can sign more. A signed non-pass is never
acceptable as a pass: every verifier (`verifySignedRecord`, and through it `verifyReceipt` and `screenReceipt`) refuses it as
`not_passing` unless its caller explicitly asks for it, and today only `clouseau review`, checking the receipt it has just
signed, asks. `clouseau review` never reviews the same revision again once it has a signed review that requires a human;
it stops and says so. To sign again, the author commits (an empty commit is enough) and reviews the new head, which must
retain or resolve the earlier findings.

**Until CI holds such a receipt for a maintainer, the setting is dark and fails closed.** CI does not ask for the signed
non-pass: the assessment, the gate and `operation: attested` refuse the receipt as `not_passing`, exactly as they refuse any
failing review. An optional-mode repository ignores it and reviews the change itself; a repository that requires a receipt
reports `review_incomplete` (`local_receipt_required`). Nothing is approved or merged on its strength, and a maintainer's
`/approve-intent` does not clear its findings.

### A receipt that does not verify is ignored

CI applies one rule to a local review receipt. A receipt that verifies in every
respect is trusted. Any receipt that does not verify is ignored: it is never
consulted again, CI runs the normal hosted review checks itself, and the pull
request shows one fixed notice. No receipt problem remains a hard failure
(`review_incomplete`). The safety argument: an ignored receipt cannot approve
anything, and CI then performs every check it would perform without a receipt
(independent tests, exact coverage, source, policy and the full hosted review), so
ignoring a receipt can never lower the bar.

The notice is `Local review receipt not used (cause: \`receipt_<class>\`): <sentence>.`
followed by what the run did instead and numbered steps. The class is one of a fixed
set, and the sentence names only values that are safe to show (a short commit id, the
engine revision, the base that moved, a changed file of the pull request, an expiry
time), never receipt contents or untrusted text. [Notices and their causes](notices.md)
lists every sentence and step:

| Class | Receipt problem |
| --- | --- |
| `malformed` | Marker, envelope, fields or JSON are malformed, unsupported, duplicated, or installation-only evidence |
| `unavailable` | The immutable artifact is missing, oversized, truncated or substituted |
| `signature` | Unknown, revoked or invalid signing key or signature |
| `author` | The signing identity is not enrolled for the PR author |
| `attestation` | An attested receipt the protected `local_review.attest` setting does not permit for this author and pull request |
| `expired` | Expired, not yet valid or an invalid challenge |
| `revision_repository` | Issued for a different repository |
| `revision_head` | Issued for a different head (both short ids are named) |
| `revision_base` | Issued against a base that has since moved (both short ids are named; step: `gh pr update-branch N`) |
| `changed` | The protected policy or configuration changed after issue (which one is named) |
| `source` | Signed sources, file inventory or diff differ from the pull request (including a changed lockfile summary) |
| `record` | The record, its digest, history, chunked structure or claimed decision is inconsistent or incomplete |
| `engine` | Produced by a different engine revision than the protected one (both short ids are named) |
| `not_passing` | The review it records did not pass |
| `settings` | The protected chunked review configuration is invalid, so the receipt cannot be checked |
| `untested`, `integrity`, `completeness` | Its evidence does not meet hosted approval's affirmative-evidence rule; the rule and, where it applies, the files are named |

Two more classes are only ever shown when no receipt can be used at all:
`absent` (the description carries no marker) and `unread` (a hosted fallback run
does not read receipts). Repositories in `required` mode have no hosted review to
fall back to. The notice then says `This repository requires a valid receipt, so
nothing is approved until you do the following.` and the outcome is
`local_receipt_required`; no provider call is made. On the receipt-only route
(`local_receipt_unusable`) the reason itself carries the cause sentence. While tests are pending or failing, an ignored receipt behaves exactly like
an unstamped change (the pending or blocked result carries the notice).

#### Manual hosted review (opt-in)

The protected top-level `hosted_review` in `.github/clouseau.json` on the base branch says whether the CI AI review of a pull
request with no usable receipt starts by itself:

| `hosted_review` | No usable receipt (absent, expired or otherwise unusable) |
| --- | --- |
| absent or `"automatic"` | today's behavior: the CI AI review runs (optional mode), or `local_receipt_required` (required mode) |
| `"manual"` | `review_incomplete`, cause `hosted_review_manual`, no provider call, until a maintainer requests the review |

The request reaches the engine only through the repository workflow: its `issue_comment` condition must start a run for
`/hosted-review ` comments, as `examples/consumer-ci.yml` does. The engine never sees a comment that starts no run, so it
cannot detect a workflow without that trigger; the hold notice therefore names the missing condition as its last step. A
consumer that sets `hosted_review: "manual"` adds the condition in the same change.

The request is a comment `/hosted-review <head sha>` on the pull request, validated as `/approve-intent` is: the exact current
head, a real user (not a bot), write permission or higher, and re-read by the engine itself from the pull request's comments.
How the run was started never matters, only such a comment. With a valid request the run proceeds as `"automatic"` would; a
request for an older head, from a reader or from a bot is ignored. A valid receipt is used whatever the setting, and a
repository in `required` mode keeps `local_receipt_required`. The receipt-only job still holds no provider secret: in manual
mode it returns `local_receipt_unusable` only when a valid request exists, so the reference workflow's hosted fallback below
starts exactly then, and the hosted job checks the request again. In the reference workflow (`examples/consumer-ci.yml`) a
`/hosted-review ` comment starts the reassessment the same way `/approve-intent ` does (the engine's `request-reassessment`
accepts an exact-head `/hosted-review` from a maintainer as it accepts `/approve-intent`); a consumer carrying an older copy adds
`|| startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/hosted-review ')` to its `request-reassessment` job condition.

#### Hosted review after an unusable receipt (reference consumer workflow)

A workflow that routes a PR whose description carries a receipt marker to a
`verify-local` job holds no provider credential in that job: the secret must not
be exposed to a job that runs on a contributor-supplied receipt. When that job finds
an optional-mode receipt unusable (decision `review_incomplete`, cause
`local_receipt_unusable`) the same run continues in a separate `assess-hosted` job
that holds the provider secrets. It runs `assess` with `ignore-receipt: 'true'`, so
the receipt is never read there, and it receives only the PR number and the frozen
engine, never an assessment, notice or record from the receipt-only job. Its
assessment and review record replace the receipt-only job's in `approve-and-merge`,
`apply-repair` and `finalize-merge`, so exactly one acceptance record is consumed per
head. A valid receipt skips the job entirely and no provider call is made. A
repository in `required` mode reports `local_receipt_required` and has no fallback.
The "receipt not used" notice is not shown on the fallback path because the
hosted job deliberately does not know why the receipt was unusable; the receipt-only
job log still carries the warning annotation naming the cause. The owner no longer
needs to remove the marker to obtain the CI review.

Deliberately unchanged, because they are intent and infrastructure rather than
receipt verification: a verified receipt still cannot replace changed review
history or supply protected-control owner authorization (the controller holds,
and the notice now names which rule: cause `receipt_protected_controls` or
`receipt_history_changed`);
a GitHub outage, rate limit or permission error while reading the receipt is
reported with its ordinary cause, not ignored; and the post-assessment gate
re-verifies the exact accepted record immediately before approval or merge and
refuses (it does not fall back) if that record no longer verifies, in which case
the next run assesses afresh.

### Protected files make a receipt unusable in CI

A change to any protected control path (the CI workflow, `.github/ci/`,
`.github/clouseau.json`, CODEOWNERS, `.clouseau-local.json`, the repository
policy file, `AGENTS.md`, and the configured `sensitive_paths`) needs the owner's
confirmation (`/approve-intent <head sha>` from the configured maintainer). It names the
exact head, unless the protected `local_review.confirmation: "diff"` lets a confirmation of an
earlier head of the same normalized diff, against an unchanged base configuration and contract,
stand for it (see above). A receipt can never grant it, so CI holds such a PR as `review_incomplete` with
cause `receipt_protected_controls` and a reason naming the protected controls.
`clouseau review` and `clouseau publish` print the same condition as a
`warning:` on stderr and a `warnings` entry in their JSON result, naming only
the repository paths. This includes the mandatory agent-standard updater commit
(`chore(agents): sync managed rules ...`), which rewrites `AGENTS.md`: keep it
local and unpushed, or push it on its own PR with a maintainer confirmation,
rather than riding on an ordinary change.
A repository that enrolls `managed_agents` in its protected configuration is exempt for
that file when the update is verifiably only the central managed block; see
[managed-standard AGENTS.md updates](managed-agents.md).

Reviewers may request `.clouseau-ci/` paths to inspect their own frozen public
engine. The collector records that engine revision as untrusted source evidence
without requiring a consumer CI checkout. CI verifies the exact signed excerpt
against its accepted engine; engine source cannot become a repository contract.


The local reuse assessment does not grant protected-control owner confirmation.
That exact-head confirmation remains mandatory in CI before approval (under the protected `local_review.confirmation: "diff"`,
a confirmation of an earlier head of the same unchanged diff also counts; see the binding section). Its pending
execution alone cannot block the pre-PR reuse assessment when the implementation
preserves the gate. Actual unsupported scope or authority still blocks.

For explicit additional behavioral checks, pass `--additional-checks FILE`, where
FILE is an operator-supplied JSON array of at most eight argv arrays, for example
`[["npm", "test", "--prefix", ".github/tests"]]`. Keep this file outside the source
checkout. This only adds checks: additional commands run after the accepted-base
recipe and native measurement, even when coverage is partial or unavailable.
They must leave the observed coverage artifacts unchanged; rewriting an artifact
is an integrity failure, not a route to better counters. Every actual command
result and the additional plan are bound to the review and cache identity. This can record consumer workflow-test execution without
changing application scripts or triggering deployment. It requires no CI keys
and creates no CI installation. Independent hosted checks remain mandatory.

Local harness presentation preserves every source byte and prior observation.
It sends verbatim source with indexed proof coordinates and replaces a duplicate
draft quote only when the identical bytes remain in the referenced immutable
source. Differing or unavailable earlier literals remain explicit. No source,
concern, disposition or score is truncated to fit transport. Oversized Codex
input fails before invocation. Native stdout/stderr are decoded across UTF-8
stream boundaries, preserving characters split between process writes. Failed
harness exits retain the final 2,000 UTF-16 code units (never starting inside a surrogate pair, so a tail may be one unit shorter) of stdout and stderr, complete
stdout character/UTF-8 byte counts and digest, elapsed time, exit status/signal,
configured bounds and controller timeout/output-limit kill reasons in private
`failure.json` beside the snapshot and journal. The stdout tail is explicitly
partial diagnostic data, never a completed review or replacement source evidence.
Public errors show only the diagnostic digest and evidence path, never the
private output or environment. Existing invocation limits remain unchanged.

CI accepts complete receipt artifacts up to 3,000,000 UTF-8 bytes. This bounded
allowance accommodates complete source and converged independent reviews without
discarding draft evidence; the prior 2 MB allowance rejected a passing 2.1 MB
consumer record. Signature envelopes use the same byte limit.
When the [GitHub Contents API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/contents#get-repository-content)
omits inline content above 1 MB, CI reads the Git blob named by that immutable
artifact's metadata. It checks the exact blob identity, byte count and Git object
hash before the normal signature, source, policy and engine verification.
Unavailable, oversized or substituted content makes the receipt ignored (class
`unavailable`); this transport does not grant trust or change receipt compatibility.
A partitioned review record too large for one receipt is stored as a signed multi-part receipt
(`clouseau-review.part-NNNN` files beside the envelope, see `docs/chunked-record.md`); each file keeps this bound.
A missing or unreadable part, or a part that does not join to the signed root, is the same `unavailable` or `record` class.

## Chunked local review

`clouseau review` (and `respond`/`publish`, which continue and publish the same review) never refuses a change for its size.
It collects the change as before; when the complete evidence does not fit one 900,000-character snapshot (or a changed file is
over 300,000 bytes) it re-collects without a cap and takes the chunked path end to end: partition (`clouseau-partition/1`), bounded unit views
(a file too large for one unit is split into segments), both roles on every unit through the unchanged reviewer, controller-computed
seams, one blind integration pass per role (none when there are no seams), merge, one grading round per role, one chunked record (`version 3`, multi-part
when it exceeds one receipt) and ONE signed receipt. A change that fits is reviewed and signed exactly as before (record `version 2`,
byte-identical). CI verifies a chunked receipt through the same single derivation, recomputing the partition, views and seams.

It is on by default. The protected `local_review.chunked` object (in `.github/clouseau.json` on the base branch, so CI reads the same
values) can only **tighten** it:

| field | meaning | bound |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled: false` | turn chunked review off; an oversized change fails as it did before | |
| `force: true` | chunk even a change that fits one snapshot | |
| `params: {C, S}` | unit ceiling and shared context | at most 450000 and 100000 |
| `concurrency` | harness sessions at once (an `--agent` review answers one at a time) | at most 2 |
| `unit_deadline_ms` | deadline of one session | at most 300000 |
| `integration_cap` | integration session input | at most 250000 |
| `integration_call_seams` | seams one integration session is given (more seams, more sessions) | at most 60 |
| `integration_max_seams` | seams the integration pass examines at all; the rest are recorded `missing` and hold approval | at most 400 |

No argument or environment variable changes them. A unit that misses the deadline stops the review with `unit_deadline` and the
ceiling to use; lower `params.C` in the protected configuration and review again. A crashed headless review resumes from its journal
(`<cache>/chunked/journal`) without sampling a finished call again. Rollback is unsetting `force` or setting `enabled: false`.

The hosted CI review has its own dark, opt-in counterpart for a pull request that has no usable receipt: see `docs/chunked-hosted.md` (`acceptance.chunked_hosted`).

## Review partition

`src/review-partition.cjs` implements scheme `clouseau-partition/1`, the first stage of reviewing a change
whose complete evidence exceeds the 900,000-character snapshot budget in bounded units. It is deterministic
and model-free; `clouseau review` uses it for a change that does not fit one snapshot.

Changed files are sorted by new path (UTF-8 bytes) and grouped into atoms: a file stays with its `.test`,
`.spec` and `.stories` siblings, a test in a separate tests tree (`test_x.py`, `x_test.py`, `x.spec.ts`) stays with the one changed source named `x` (no pairing when zero or several sources carry that name), and a rename is one entry keyed by its new path. A file costs
`ceil(1.03 * (base bytes + head bytes + patch characters))`, where the patch size is the stored one (a file added whole keeps only its patch header, its body lives once in the head source). Atoms are packed next-fit, in path order, into
units of at most `unit_ceiling` (C = 450,000); an atom above C becomes its own unit. The plan digest covers the
scheme, parameters, unit membership and costs, so it is the same for any input order. Every changed path is
owned by exactly one unit (checked by `checkOwnership`).

A change is never refused for its size, and never truncated. The plan refuses only what is not a size: an
`unpartitionable_path`, an `unpartitionable_binary` (binary changes still fail closed), a duplicate path, or an
inconsistent ownership. A file with a `derived_size` (a lockfile replaced by a summary CI can recompute) costs that summary
instead of its sources. Every entry also costs `file_overhead` (512 characters, its accounting entry and manifest row), so a
thousand tiny files fill units as a few large ones do.

The number of units is unbounded (the runner executes them in waves). A stem group (a file and its tests) costing more than
`budget - shared - reserve` (900,000 - 100,000 - 240,000 = 560,000) falls apart into its files; a file costing more than that
is split into **segments** of at most C (`src/file-segments.cjs`). Every unit view stays inside the 900,000 budget.

A segment owns a contiguous run of the file's patch rows, so every changed line belongs to exactly one segment, and one
unit per segment (two segments of one file never share a unit). Its view shows that segment's patch (with sub-hunk headers
that count exactly its rows) and, as ordinary sources, the windows of the base and head text the rows touch plus 12 lines of
margin (a file added whole is stored compactly, its body once, in the head window). Windows keep the file's line structure:
the first line of a window is line `segment.start_line` of the whole source. A single line larger than a fragment (a minified
bundle) is cut into consecutive pieces owned by consecutive segments. The merge lifts every citation of a window to the same
lines of the whole source, which holds because a quote is a piece of the lines it cites, so the merged report is validated by
the unchanged validators against the complete combined snapshot. A unit's spec names its segment as
`parts: {path: {index, count}}`; `checkOwnership` and the record verifier want every index of `0..count-1` exactly once.
Inconsistent evidence (a patch that names a line outside its source) is an integrity error (`segment_inconsistent`), never a guess.

The change manifest every unit receives lists every changed path while it fits 60,000 characters. Beyond that the deepest
directories are summarized first (`{dir, files, additions, deletions, size, units}`, `unit_count` when more than 16 units), then
shallower ones, down to one row for the whole change; the files a unit owns are listed in full in its own files. Optional shared
context beyond the shared cap (another unit's lockfile summary, an engine file) is dropped and listed in `shared_omitted`;
only the contracts, the verification record and the request are mandatory, and those must fit the shared cap. That limit is a
property of the repository's contract documents, not of the size of a change.

`src/change-table.cjs` reads the planner's table from the stored snapshot, costing text by its JSON-escaped length, and adds
the segment costs of a file too large for a unit, so the plan, CI's recomputation and the views agree.

Print a plan for a table of changed files (`{files: [{path, previous?, base_size, head_size, patch_chars,
derived_size?}]}`; `test/fixtures/alcantara-02618a9.json` is the measured table of alcantara commit 02618a9,
which gives 4 units at C = 450,000 with stored sizes, 5 when every added file also counts its full patch). A table has only
sizes, so a file too large for a unit is split into equal parts:

```
scripts/partition-plan test/fixtures/alcantara-02618a9.json [--ceiling 300000]
```

The parameters come from the protected `local_review.chunked` configuration (defaults C = 450,000, S = 100,000). The earlier `max_units` and `file_ceiling` parameters, and the protected `cap` and `max_units`, bound
nothing any more (the protected configuration still accepts `cap` and `max_units` and ignores them).

### Unbounded collection

`collectLocal({..., unbounded: true})` is the collector of a chunked review: a changed file, a patch or the combined
snapshot of any size is read whole (binary evidence still fails closed), and the optional engine seed is never omitted for
size. Without the option nothing changes: one snapshot of at most 900,000 characters. The combined snapshot is reviewed in
bounded views and stored as a multi-part receipt (`docs/chunked-record.md`).

### Alcantara-shaped measurement

`scripts/measure-chunked [TABLE.json] [--ceiling N] [--shared N]` builds a synthetic
change from a table (fictional filler content of exactly the measured sizes, a real derived lockfile summary, compact
added files), partitions it, builds every unit view, merges fake finding-free unit reports, builds the thin chunked
record, signs it with an ephemeral key and verifies it through the one derivation. It prints the unit count,
per-unit sizes (view, owned, shared, manifest, foreign hunks, estimated prompt), the record size against the single-receipt
limit and the signed receipt (one file, or a multi-part receipt) size, then runs the real unit runner against a fake harness and prints the
EXACT prompt characters of every unit and integration session. No AI, network or secret is used. For `02618a9`
it gives 4 units, a 1.55M combined snapshot, a 1.70M record (59.5% of the single-receipt limit) and a largest estimated prompt of about 570K characters.
`src/chunked-measure.test.cjs` asserts these bounds and that every size which used to be refused (170 files, more than 8 units,
a record over the signing limit, roughly 500 paths, a file over 300,000 bytes, a unit over the unit budget, a file of
millions of characters, a single line of a million) is partitioned, reviewed, merged, signed and verified.

# Receipt compatibility across engine revisions

A signed local review receipt names the engine revision that produced it (`reviewer_sha`, `reviewer_digest`). Today CI
accepts it only when that is exactly the protected `main` it resolved. `main` moves many times a day, so a receipt
rots within hours and CI repeats a review (about $6 and several minutes) even when the engine change cannot affect what
the review attests. This design lets CI accept a receipt issued under revision X while running revision Y, if and only if
Y itself declares X's review semantics compatible. If CI cannot establish that, it behaves as it does today: the receipt is
ignored and CI reviews.

## Design

**Review-semantics digest.** `src/review-semantics.cjs` hashes every engine file under the same roots as the exact engine
digest (`action.yml`, `src`, `policy`, `bin`, `skills`, `scripts`; tests excluded) *except* the files listed in its
`NEUTRAL` table. Each neutral file has a written reason. A file is semantic by default: a new or renamed file is part of
the meaning until a person lists it as neutral. The table lives in `review-semantics.cjs`, which is itself semantic, so
moving a file into it changes the digest and forces the same decision as editing the file would.

**Compatibility statement.** `policy/review-compatibility.json` is in-tree on protected main:

```json
{"version": 1, "current": "<digest of this tree>", "compatible": ["<older digest>", "..."]}
```

`current` must equal the digest of the tree that contains it. `compatible` lists earlier semantics whose receipts this
tree accepts (at most 64, newest first, never including `current`). The statement is the only source of compatibility.

Two further files exist only to keep the statement in step with the tree, and `acceptor()` never reads them:

- `compat/manifest.json` lists the semantic files (path, executable bits, content hash) the statement was last folded for.
  Its digest must equal `current`. It lets a tool say which semantic files changed since the fold by comparing two file
  lists, with no Git history.
- `compat/declarations/<digest>.json`, one file per pull request, state that a set of semantic files changed (by content
  hash, or deleted) and whether the change is `compatible` or `incompatible`. A declaration is inert until it is folded.

**Receipt.** A receipt additionally signs `reviewer_semantics`, the digest of the engine that issued it. Receipts without
the field behave exactly as before.

**Acceptance.** `verifySignedRecord` keeps every check it has (enrolled key, author, expiry, record binding, repository,
head, base, policy and configuration digests, recomputed decision, passing result). Only when the exact engine comparison
fails, and only in central-source mode, it asks `acceptor()` whether the receipt's `reviewer_semantics` is acceptable.
`acceptor()` reads the statement from the engine checkout that is running, the checkout `identifyEngine` and
`verifyEngine` already bound to the SHA the resolver read from protected `gaulatti/clouseau` `main`. It answers yes only
if the statement parses, `current` equals the digest it computes from that checkout, and the claim is `current` or listed.
Everything else answers no.

## Declare, then fold

A pull request never rewrites the statement. Two pull requests that each change semantic files therefore never touch the
same line, and merge in either order without a manual re-bump.

**In the pull request.** When semantic files change, `src/review-semantics.test.cjs` (the required `verify` job) fails with
"Undeclared review-semantics change" until the author records the decision, which adds one new file:

- `scripts/review-compatibility declare --compatible`: the change cannot alter what a review attests (refactor, comment,
  performance, a notice). Earlier receipts stay acceptable.
- `scripts/review-compatibility declare --incompatible`: the change alters rubrics, prompts, schema, scoring, validation,
  source selection, receipt format or anything else a review means. Every earlier receipt is ignored and CI reviews, which
  is the safe default for doubt.

The declaration names each changed semantic file with its content hash (a deleted file as `sha256: null`). The file is named
by the digest of its own content. `verify` passes only when every changed semantic file is covered by exactly one
declaration whose hash equals the file in the tree, and every declaration covers a file that really changed. An undeclared
change, a declaration for a file that did not change, a file changed again after it was declared, two declarations for one
file, an unknown file in `compat/declarations/` and a manifest that does not match the statement all fail `verify`.

**On protected main.** `scripts/review-compatibility fold` turns the declarations into the new statement and manifest and

# Clouseau review contract

Clouseau provides shared, evidence-bound repository change assessment, exact
coverage gates, native PR approval and merge, and deployment-driven wiki updates.
Consumers provide their own protected purpose contract and verification steps.

Local agent review and authenticated receipt reuse serve the same change
acceptance purpose. Agent-only installation and refresh are independent of CI
installation. A protected verifier may reuse an enrolled runner's source-bound
passing review without another AI request, while preserving native tests, exact
coverage, existing owner authority and branch protection. Initial workstation
signing explicitly trusts the enrolled operator and privileged processes; it
does not claim hardware attestation or protection from a compromised runner.

Changes must preserve the trust boundary between untrusted contributor source,
secret-free execution checks, read-only AI evaluation and the separate write
controller. Native protected-main requirements, immutable revision identities,
meaningful tests and exact 100% line and branch coverage are mandatory.
Model text is data. It must never execute as a command or grant permissions.

An explicitly accepted manual-only integration must enforce branch protection
where GitHub makes it available and disable automatic merge for every author.
GitHub's documented private-plan protection limitation may permit independent
review and approval without host-enforced merge blocking, but never automatic
merge, waived tests, lowered coverage or omitted current-head owner approval for
external contributions. Missing credentials or generic API failures are not
evidence of that plan limitation. Report the enforcement boundary truthfully.

Useful defect repairs, meaningful tests, provider qualification and maintenance
serve this purpose without a new product decision. Speculative frameworks,
unrelated capabilities or additional authority require concrete justification.
The shared protocol defines product and technical scoring; no owner intent
confirmation waives integrity failures, incomplete evidence or technical defects.

Changes to the reviewer implementation, scoring policy, verification controls or
this purpose contract require explicit exact-revision confirmation from gaulatti.
Only real purpose, authority and outcome tradeoffs are sent to the owner. A
missing provider response or unresolved code concern belongs to automated
investigation or bounded repair, never automatic approval.

Declarations chain: after A to B and B to C were both declared compatible, A's receipts are accepted under C. When two pull
requests are folded together, their combined step is compatible only if both declared `compatible`. If a series of small
changes could add up to a different review, declare the last one incompatible. After about 50 further `compatible` folds the
64-entry cap drops the oldest digests and receipts issued under them are ignored again.

Two pull requests that edit the **same** semantic file are the one case that still needs a second declaration: Git may merge
the text, but the merged content then matches neither declaration, so `verify` fails until one author deletes their
declaration and declares again. That is the safe direction. Where the protected `local_review.binding: "diff"` applies, the
second declaration does not void the pull request's diff-bound receipt as long as it keeps the same verdict over the same
files: CI compares declarations by what they declare, not by the digests they pin (see
[binding a receipt to its diff](local-review.md#binding-a-receipt-to-its-diff-opt-in)).

## Why the list cannot go stale silently (the enforcement argument)

The risk is a semantic change that nobody declared, so that CI accepts a receipt from a weaker or different review. The
argument has four steps.

1. The digest is a function of the bytes of the semantic files, so any semantic change changes it. Reverting restores the
   old digest, which is sound because the bytes are identical.
2. The statement is rejected unless `current` equals the digest of its own tree (`acceptor()`; unchanged by the declare
   and fold flow). The engine's required `verify` job asserts that every semantic file that differs from the manifest is
   covered by exactly one valid declaration, so a change to a semantic file cannot merge without a visible
   `--compatible` or `--incompatible` decision bound to that file's content. Between the merge and the fold, `current`
   no longer equals the digest of the tree, so `acceptor()` answers no to everything: receipts are ignored and CI reviews.
   Only the fold turns a decision into a statement, and it applies the same checks as `verify`.
3. Default-semantic classification closes the "unclassified file" gap: adding a file, renaming one or editing the neutral
   table all change the digest. Listing a file as neutral requires a reason, and the test fails if semantic code loads or
   names any neutral file (apart from `src/cli-usage.cjs`, marked presentation), so a dependency cannot be mislabelled
   neutral by accident.
4. The statement, the manifest, the declarations, the module, the test and every other file under `src/`, `policy/`,
   `compat/`, `scripts/`, `bin/` and `skills/` are protected review controls (`sensitive_paths`). A change to them already needs the owner's exact-revision confirmation.
   The enforcement is a ratchet that makes the owner's compatibility decision unavoidable and visible, not a technical lock
   against an owner who approves a wrong declaration.

There is deliberately a window between a merge and its fold in which main's statement is stale. It is safe because
`acceptor()` refuses everything then (receipts are ignored and CI reviews), and it is short: the fold follows the merge's
review workflow, any push that touches `compat/declarations/`, and a half-hourly schedule. If a fold cannot run or fails,
the window stays open and CI keeps reviewing; nothing is ever accepted on the strength of an unfolded declaration.

# Clouseau review contract

Clouseau provides shared, evidence-bound repository change assessment, exact
coverage gates, native PR approval and merge, and deployment-driven wiki updates.
Consumers provide their own protected purpose contract and verification steps.

Local agent review and authenticated receipt reuse serve the same change
acceptance purpose. Agent-only installation and refresh are independent of CI
installation. A protected verifier may reuse an enrolled runner's source-bound
passing review without another AI request, while preserving native tests, exact
coverage, existing owner authority and branch protection. Initial workstation
signing explicitly trusts the enrolled operator and privileged processes; it
does not claim hardware attestation or protection from a compromised runner.

Changes must preserve the trust boundary between untrusted contributor source,
secret-free execution checks, read-only AI evaluation and the separate write
controller. Native protected-main requirements, immutable revision identities,
meaningful tests and exact 100% line and branch coverage are mandatory.
Model text is data. It must never execute as a command or grant permissions.

An explicitly accepted manual-only integration must enforce branch protection
where GitHub makes it available and disable automatic merge for every author.
GitHub's documented private-plan protection limitation may permit independent
review and approval without host-enforced merge blocking, but never automatic
merge, waived tests, lowered coverage or omitted current-head owner approval for
external contributions. Missing credentials or generic API failures are not
evidence of that plan limitation. Report the enforcement boundary truthfully.

Useful defect repairs, meaningful tests, provider qualification and maintenance
serve this purpose without a new product decision. Speculative frameworks,
unrelated capabilities or additional authority require concrete justification.
The shared protocol defines product and technical scoring; no owner intent
confirmation waives integrity failures, incomplete evidence or technical defects.

Changes to the reviewer implementation, scoring policy, verification controls or
this purpose contract require explicit exact-revision confirmation from gaulatti.
Only real purpose, authority and outcome tradeoffs are sent to the owner. A
missing provider response or unresolved code concern belongs to automated
investigation or bounded repair, never automatic approval.
